title: China ports hit record 7.3m TEU in one week
metaDescription: Chinese ports handled 7.3m TEU in a week, up 9% year on year. Tariff uncertainty ahead of Trump-Xi summit drove the surge. How it changes your Q4 plan.
bottomLine: Chinese ports handled a record 7.3 million TEU in the week ending 20 September, 9% above last year and accelerating from 6% earlier this month. The surge preceded the Trump-Xi summit and appears driven by exporters rushing goods ahead of possible tariff increases. If you have Q4 inventory in a factory right now, you are not alone and the freight schedule reflects that.

stories.headline: China ports moved record 7.3m TEU in week to 20 Sept
stories.tldr: Chinese ports handled 7.3 million TEU in the week ending 20 September, up 9% year on year and the busiest week in history.
stories.whatHappened:
Chinese ports handled 7.3 million TEU in the seven days ending 20 September, according to China's Ministry of Transport. The volume was 9% higher than the same week in 2025 and the busiest week in the ports' history. The increase accelerated from 6% growth in the first two weeks of September.

The surge preceded the Trump-Xi summit in Washington. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on 24 September that the two countries agreed to extend their trade truce by two months to 10 January 2027. The Trump administration had intended to release a report recommending a 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods before the summit.
stories.whyItMatters:
You are competing for vessel slots and warehouse capacity with everyone else who read the same tariff headlines. The 9% year-on-year increase means your freight rate is unlikely to fall before Golden Week, and your carrier is less likely to absorb a late booking without a premium.

If you planned to book space for November delivery, that space is tighter than the headline rate suggests. Carriers blank sailings around Golden Week, but they are cancelling fewer voyages than usual because cargo demand remains firm. That keeps rates elevated but does not guarantee your container makes the sailing you want.

The two-month extension to 10 January removes the immediate tariff trigger, but it does not remove the behaviour. Factories are still pushing goods out, buyers are still front-loading, and the resulting volume keeps your lead time longer than the transit time alone would suggest.
stories.hotTake: The record week is not a one-off, it is the third consecutive month of double-digit export growth and the fastest pace since the pandemic peaks. The extension buys two months, but it does not reverse the inventory already afloat or the bookings already made. If your Q1 plan assumed rates would fall in November, revise it.
actions: Pull your Q4 forecast forward and confirm bookings for late October departures now, before Golden Week blank sailings compress available slots further.
Check your carrier's blank sailing schedule for the first two weeks of October and rebook any cargo at risk of rolling to the following week.
Revise your Q1 freight budget to assume rates hold at current levels through year-end rather than falling after peak season.

stories.headline: Jiangyin opens direct container service to Mexico
stories.tldr: Jiangyin port launched a direct container route to Manzanillo on 24 September with a 22-day transit, cutting transshipment time via Shanghai or Ningbo.
stories.whatHappened:
A cargo ship carrying 524 containers departed Jiangyin port in Jiangsu province on 24 September for Manzanillo, Mexico. The voyage marks the launch of a direct container service between Jiangsu and Mexico. The route operates as a direct service with a transit time of approximately 22 days.

Most containers on the inaugural voyage use a lowered-profile design to meet height restrictions in Mexican railway tunnels and under bridges. The containers can be transferred directly between railway flatcars and truck chassis for road-rail intermodal transport across North America.
stories.whyItMatters:
You now have a routing option that skips Shanghai and Ningbo, which matters if those ports are congested or if your goods move onward by rail in Mexico. The 22-day direct transit is faster than transshipment, and the intermodal containers reduce your inland costs if your final destination is beyond the port.

The service opens Yangtze River factories to Mexico without forcing you through the Shanghai gateway. If your supplier is in Jiangsu and your buyer is in Mexico or the southern United States, this route cuts days and handling fees from your delivered cost.

The catch is that a new service has no track record. You do not know the carrier's schedule reliability, the port's equipment availability, or how well the intermodal handoff works in practice. The first sailing proves the route exists, not that it works reliably under load.
stories.hotTake: Direct routes from secondary Chinese ports to secondary foreign ports are almost always better in theory than in practice. The transit time looks good, the handling cost looks good, and then the vessel skips a sailing or the port runs out of chassis. Test it with a small shipment before you move your entire Mexico programme onto an unproven lane.
actions: Test the Jiangyin-Manzanillo route with a single container on the next available sailing and track door-to-door transit time including inland legs.
Ask your freight forwarder for the carrier's schedule reliability data once three sailings have completed, and compare it to your current routing via Shanghai.
Calculate your total delivered cost including inland transport in Mexico for both the direct route and transshipment via a major gateway before committing volume.

stories.headline: Asia-US West Coast rates up 4% to $8,100 per FEU
stories.tldr: Spot rates from Asia to the U.S. West Coast rose 4% last week to above $8,100 per FEU, while East Coast rates held at $9,600.
stories.whatHappened:
Spot rates from Asia to the U.S. West Coast increased 4% last week to more than $8,100 per forty-foot equivalent unit. East Coast rates were essentially unchanged at about $9,600 per FEU.

The elevated levels reflect strong cargo demand, weather-related port congestion in the Far East, and carrier capacity management through blank sailings. Cancellation data points to relatively firm demand compared with prior years, suggesting carriers have less need to withdraw capacity than they typically would as the traditional peak-season window closes.
stories.whyItMatters:
Your ocean freight cost is not falling before November, and it may not fall then either. The 4% increase on the Transpacific contradicts the usual September pattern, when rates start to decline as peak season ends. Carriers are blanking sailings, but they are blanking fewer than usual because cargo volumes remain strong.

If you planned your Q4 budget assuming rates would drop in October, you are now paying 10% to 15% more than forecast. The $8,100 West Coast rate and $9,600 East Coast rate are two to three times the pre-pandemic normal, and they are holding because demand is holding.

The real problem is not the rate, it is the uncertainty. You do not know if carriers will add capacity after Golden Week or if blank sailings will tighten further. That makes it harder to lock in a rate for Q1 and harder to forecast your landed cost three months out.
stories.hotTake: The Transpacific market is defying the usual seasonal pattern, and that tells you more about cargo volume than it does about carrier behaviour. Rates do not stay high in October unless boxes are moving. If your competitors are shipping at these rates, they have either priced it in or they are losing money. Make sure you know which one you are.
actions: Lock in Q4 freight rates now with a contract or a series of spot bookings rather than waiting for a drop that may not come.
Recalculate your Q4 margin assuming $8,100 West Coast and $9,600 East Coast rates hold through November, and identify which SKUs stop being profitable.
Ask your freight forwarder for weekly rate updates through October and set a threshold at which you pause orders or raise prices.

stories.headline: US and China extend trade truce to 10 January
stories.tldr: The U.S. and China agreed to extend their trade truce by two months to 10 January 2027, delaying any new tariff decisions until after the summit.
stories.whatHappened:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on 24 September that the United States and China agreed to extend their trade truce by two months to 10 January 2027. The original agreement, set to expire 10 November 2026, lowered certain tariffs and suspended trade actions.

The Trump administration had intended to release a report before the summit recommending a 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods. That report and any related tariff action are now delayed. Bessent said he was unsure if a larger deal could be reached by 10 January or if the countries would extend the current agreement further.
stories.whyItMatters:
You have two more months of known tariff rates, which means you can forecast your landed cost through year-end without the risk of a surprise 7.5% increase. The extension removes the immediate threat, but it does not remove the long-term uncertainty. The tariff decision is delayed, not cancelled.

If you front-loaded inventory in August and September to beat the expected tariff increase, you now have more stock than you needed and your competitors who waited have the same tariff rate you do. The extension rewards the cautious and penalises the aggressive, at least in the short term.

The 10 January deadline falls after Chinese New Year factory shutdowns start. That means if tariffs do increase in January, you will have limited time to bring forward shipments before factories close for the holiday. The extension bought you two months, but it compressed your response window.
stories.hotTake: The extension is a relief for Q4 planning but a headache for Q1. You now face the same decision in January that you faced in September, except you will have less time to react and factories will be closing for New Year. If the tariff threat was real enough to front-load in September, it is real enough to plan for in January. Do not waste the two months.
actions: Revise your Q1 order schedule to assume a 7.5% tariff increase takes effect 10 January and pull forward any shipments that would otherwise depart in late January or February.
Calculate your cost impact from a 7.5% tariff increase on your China-sourced SKUs and identify which products become unviable at that rate.
Ask your freight forwarder and customs broker what the lead time is for a January shipment if you place the order in November, factoring in Chinese New Year closures.

contentHooks: Chinese ports handled 7.3 million TEU in one week, the busiest ever, and your Q4 freight slot just got harder to book.
Everyone planned to beat the tariff deadline, so now everyone is competing for the same vessel space and the same warehouse capacity.
The two-month tariff extension to 10 January removes the Q4 threat but compresses your Q1 response window right into Chinese New Year.
Jiangyin opened a direct route to Mexico with 22-day transit, which is faster than Shanghai transshipment but has zero track record under load.
Transpac spot rates rose 4% last week when they should be falling, which tells you cargo volume is stronger than the seasonal pattern.
If your competitors are shipping at $8,100 West Coast and $9,600 East Coast, they have either priced it in or they are losing money on every container.
The record port volumes are not a spike, they are the third consecutive month of double-digit export growth and the pattern is holding.
Carriers are blanking fewer sailings than usual because demand is firm, which keeps rates high but does not guarantee your box makes the sailing.
The tariff extension rewards sellers who waited and penalises those who front-loaded inventory in August and September.
A 7.5% tariff increase in January hits you harder than the same increase in November because factories close for New Year and you have less time to react.
Testing a new shipping route with a small shipment costs you one container, committing your entire Mexico programme to an unproven lane costs you a quarter.
If you planned your Q4 budget assuming ocean rates would drop in October, you are now paying 10% to 15% more than forecast and the gap is widening.

faq.question: Why are China port volumes hitting records in September 2026?
faq.answer: Chinese ports handled 7.3 million TEU in the week ending 20 September, the busiest week in history and 9% above 2025. Exporters rushed goods ahead of possible U.S. tariff increases. The Trump administration had planned a 7.5% tariff before the summit. The two countries extended their trade truce to 10 January, but volumes remain elevated because the long-term tariff risk persists.

faq.question: What are ocean freight rates from China to the US right now?
faq.answer: Spot rates from Asia to the U.S. West Coast are above $8,100 per forty-foot container, up 4% last week. East Coast rates are about $9,600 per FEU. Rates are elevated due to strong cargo demand, port congestion in China, and carrier blank sailings ahead of Golden Week. Rates are not falling as they usually do in September because cargo volumes remain firm.

faq.question: Did the US and China agree to delay tariffs?
faq.answer: Yes. The United States and China agreed on 24 September to extend their trade truce by two months to 10 January 2027. The extension delays any new tariff decisions, including a proposed 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods. The extension gives both sides more time to negotiate but does not resolve the underlying trade issues or eliminate the threat.

faq.question: Should I book my China shipments now or wait for rates to drop?
faq.answer: Book now. Ocean freight rates from China to the U.S. rose last week when they should be falling, and carrier blank sailings are fewer than usual because demand remains strong. If you wait for rates to drop in October, you risk paying the same rate or higher while losing your preferred vessel slot.
